title: Egg white vs. yolk: what each part provides

seo.title: Egg white vs. yolk: protein, fat, calories and nutrients
seo.meta_description: Egg white concentrates protein with almost no fat; yolk provides fat and most of the egg's choline, vitamins A, D and B12, iron and phosphorus.
seo.search_intent: Compare what egg whites and yolks contribute and understand why they are not nutritionally interchangeable.

excerpt: Per 100 g, raw egg white provides about 52 calories, 10.9 g protein and 0.17 g fat; raw yolk provides about 322 calories, 15.9 g protein and 26.5 g fat. White is protein-efficient, while yolk carries most of the fat and many micronutrients.
content_html:
Separating an egg changes much more than fat content. The white is mostly water and protein; the yolk concentrates fat and many micronutrients.

Per-100-g comparison

NutrientRaw whiteRaw yolk
Calories~52~322
Protein~10.9 g~15.9 g
Fat~0.17 g~26.5 g
Iron~0.08 mg~2.7 mg
Phosphorus~15 mg~390 mg
Selenium~20 µg~56 µg

A real egg does not contain equal weights of both parts. A large egg typically has roughly 33 g white and 17 g yolk.

Protein per large egg

At those weights, one large white provides about 3.6 g protein and one yolk about 2.7 g. The white provides a little over half the egg's protein, not all of it.

Almost all fat is in the yolk

A roughly 17 g yolk contains about 4.5 g fat, while a white contributes almost none. Removing yolks therefore lowers calories and fat substantially.

Yolk carries choline and fat-soluble vitamins

USDA choline data show only about 1 mg choline/100 g in raw white versus several hundred milligrams per 100 g in yolk. Yolk also concentrates vitamins A, D and B12, iron, phosphorus and carotenoids.

When whites are useful

Extra whites are an efficient way to raise protein with little energy or fat. Whole eggs provide a broader nutrient package because the yolk contributes much of what whites lack.

White and yolk do different nutritional jobs. White excels at lean protein; yolk supplies fat, choline and much of the egg's vitamin and mineral diversity.

What changes when you use only one part

Separating eggs can be useful for recipes or for adjusting a meal, but several nutrients change at the same time. Extra whites raise protein with relatively few calories and almost no fat. Removing every yolk also removes most of the egg's choline, vitamin B12, vitamin A, vitamin D, and other nutrients associated with the yolk. A better protein-to-calorie ratio is therefore not the same thing as greater nutrient density in every category.

A common middle ground is one whole egg plus additional whites. This preserves the yolk's flavor, emulsifying properties, and micronutrients while increasing total protein. The right balance depends on the dish: an omelet, meringue, custard, and mayonnaise rely on very different functions from the two parts of the egg.

Dietary cholesterol is concentrated in the yolk. For most people, the effect of eggs is interpreted within the overall eating pattern rather than by labeling the yolk as inherently good or bad. Anyone following individualized medical advice for cholesterol or cardiovascular risk should use that guidance instead of applying a generic white-versus-yolk rule.

Food safety is shared by both portions when eggs are raw. Recipes that remain uncooked or only lightly cooked are safer when made with pasteurized eggs or pasteurized egg products, particularly for people at higher risk from foodborne illness.

Calories are distributed very unevenly as well. The white is mostly water plus protein, whereas the yolk contains the egg's fat and therefore more energy per gram. That distinction can be useful when designing a recipe, but one whole egg is still a relatively compact portion of food. Butter or oil in the pan, cheese, processed meat, toast, and other sides can change the meal's calorie and sodium content more than the decision to include one additional yolk.

For baking, separating eggs for nutrition alone can also change structure because yolk fat and emulsifiers and white proteins behave differently under heat. Recipe performance should be considered alongside nutrient targets.

The yolk also carries carotenoids such as lutein and zeaxanthin, with concentrations that can vary with the hen's diet. A deeper orange color does not provide a precise measure of vitamin content or overall egg quality, but it illustrates why the yolk is more than simply a package of fat and cholesterol.

For protein planning, it can be useful to remember that a whole large egg contains protein from both compartments. Discarding the yolk removes some protein along with its other nutrients, so replacing several whole eggs with whites changes more than the fat content. The best choice depends on the nutritional role of the entire meal rather than on one nutrient in isolation.

faq.question: Where is most egg protein?
faq.answer: A large white has about 3.6 g protein and a yolk about 2.7 g, so the white provides a little over half.

faq.question: Does egg white contain fat?
faq.answer: Very little: about 0.17 g/100 g versus about 26.5 g/100 g in yolk.

faq.question: What do you lose by removing the yolk?
faq.answer: Most fat plus much of the egg's choline, vitamins A, D and B12, iron and phosphorus.
